sections.overview: The great horned owl is a large, powerful owl found across most of the Americas. It is one of the most widespread and adaptable owls of the continent, living in almost every kind of habitat from swamps to deserts to northern forests.
sections.identification: A big owl, 46–63 cm long with a wingspan of roughly 1–1.5 m; females are larger than males. The plumage is mottled brown and black above, with barred underparts, a white throat patch and a tan or whitish face. Large feather tufts, the “horns”, rise from the head, and the eyes are yellow.
sections.habitat: It occurs from sea level to high mountains, in forests, woodlots, streamsides, grassland, deserts, marshes and even towns. In the breeding season it avoids treeless tundra and unbroken grassland, because it needs trees or heavy brush for cover.
sections.diet: It eats mostly mammals such as rabbits, rats, mice and voles, and is one of the few regular predators of skunks. It also takes birds, up to the size of a goose, reptiles, frogs, insects and, rarely, fish; more than 500 prey species have been recorded.
sections.behavior: A mostly nocturnal, solitary hunter, it watches from a high perch and then swoops on its prey. It is territorial and usually stays in the same area all year. Its song is a deep, far-carrying “ho-ho-hoo hoo hoo”, heard most after midnight.
sections.reproduction: It nests very early, sometimes in late winter in the north, usually in an old nest of another large bird. The clutch is typically 2–3 whitish eggs, incubated mainly by the female for roughly 28–37 days. Young climb onto nearby branches at about five weeks and fly at nine to ten weeks, and are fed by the parents for months.
sections.ecology: As a top predator it helps control rodent populations, and its numbers follow those of its prey, such as snowshoe hares. Adults have few natural enemies, though crows and raccoons may eat eggs and other great horned owls sometimes kill them in territorial fights.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. It is widespread and common, and numbers appear to be holding up well in most areas; the population has been estimated at about 5.7 million birds. In the wild, an average lifespan of around 13 years has been reported, with a record of 28.
